newsitem.title: GERMANY: Deutsche Telekom plays down EU cable report.
newsitem.headline: Deutsche Telekom plays down EU cable report.

text.p: German phone giant Deutsche Telekom AG on Tuesday played down a news report that said the European Commission planned to present proposals in March to force it to sell part or all of its cable television network.

An advance release of an article to appear in the latest issue of the monthly Capital said European Competition Commissioner Karel Van Miert was studying three alternative proposals to weaken Telekom's control of the cable TV market.
"We have not heard anything official about this study," Telekom spokesman Stephan Althoff told Reuters.
"And if such a study exists then it is based on false presumptions because there is harsh competition in the German cable television industry," he added.
The European Commission is preparing a study on the impact on competition of the possession of cable television networks by former telecommunications monopolies.

The study will explore whether, as in Germany, ownership of such networks by dominant carriers after liberalisation of European telecommunications next year would impede competition and what might be done to prevent this happening.
Van Miert has in the past taken a critical view of Deutsche Telekom's position in the German cable TV industry.
While there are many local cable TV operators, until recently Telekom had a monopoly on the basic cable TV networks.
As a result, it owns and operates Germany's only trunk cable TV network but has just 5.5 million of the 16 million cable TV subscribers under direct contract.

The remainder subscribe to services provided by regional operators, such as Vebacom -- the joint venture of Veba AG and Cable and Wireless, which is the number two cable operator with nearly two million subscribers.

But while competing operators can now offer services and build their own infrastructure, they are still dependent on Telekom's national cable TV network and say Telekom is delaying investment that would allow them to offer new services.
The Capital report said the Commission is discussing three alternatives to weaken Telekom's dominance of the German cable TV market and open the way for greater competition.
-- Force Telekom to divest the network altogether.
-- Place the network into a separate company and not allow Telekom to own a stake of more than 25 percent.
-- Break up the network into regional cable companies.

Deutsche Telekom is so concerned about the Commission's findings that chief executive Ron Sommer plans to meet behind closed doors later this month with German parliament's postal affairs committee, the Capital report said.

Telekom spokesman Althoff said Sommer had invited the members of the postal affairs committee to a meeting in order to outline the company's strategy for developing the cable TV network for multimedia services.

Telekom's competitors last year proposed jointly investing five billion marks to transform the Telekom's cable TV network into a so-called "full-service network" capable of delivering television and multimedia, phone services and Internet access.
But Telekom has blocked the plan and its competitors say this is exactly the reason why the Commission should get involved to weaken Telekom's grip on the market.
If the Commission forced some opening of the cable TV network it would not be the first time it did so.

Last year it forced Dutch telecoms operator KPN to sell its cable TV network to further competition. In the rest of Europe, only in Germany and Portugal do former telephone monopolies also have a cable television monopoly.
